\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Reverse iteration step]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.revStep}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.revStep}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.isNilB, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Turing.pairEncode}
For a Boolean list $S$, define one step as follows: if the first component decoded from
$S$ is empty, return $S$; otherwise, return the pair encoding of that component with its
first entry removed and the list formed by prepending its first entry (using `false` if
needed) to the second decoded component.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Reverse-step transformation is polynomial-time computable]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_revStep}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_revStep}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_cons, Complexity.BinArith.revStep, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_headD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_id, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_isNil, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_ite, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_tail}
\difficulty{3}
For a bit string $S$, return $S$ if its first decoded component is empty. Otherwise,
return the paired encoding of the tail of that component and a second component formed
by prefixing its first bit to the second decoded component of $S$; failed pair decodings
yield empty components, and the first bit of an empty list is taken to be $0$. This
function is polynomial-time computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[One Step of Reversal on Encoded Pairs]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.revStep_pairEncode}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.revStep_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.revStep, Complexity.isNilB, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{4}
For any two bit strings $u$ and $v$, there exist bit strings $u'$ and $v'$ such that
applying the specified reversal step to $\langle u,v\rangle$ gives $\langle
u',v'\rangle$, and
$\operatorname{reverse}(u')\mathbin{++}v'=\operatorname{reverse}(u)\mathbin{++}v$. Their
total length is preserved: $|u'|+|v'|=|u|+|v|$. If $u$ is nonempty, then $|u'|<|u|$; if
$u$ is empty, then $u'$ is empty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bit-string reversal is polynomial-time computable]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_reverse}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_reverse}
\leanok

\difficulty{6}
The function that sends each finite bit string to the same bits in reverse order is
polynomial-time computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Binary multiplication]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.mul}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.mul}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD}
For a Boolean list $z$, define its binary product to be the binary representation of the
product of the natural numbers represented by the two components decoded from $z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Multiplication on encoded binary expansions]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.mul_pairEncode}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.mul_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.mul, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal_bits, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, let $\operatorname{bits}(n)$ denote the bit string
representing $n$. Applying the operation that decodes a paired input, multiplies the
values of its two components, and returns the resulting bit string to the encoding of
$\operatorname{bits}(a)$ and $\operatorname{bits}(b)$ yields $\operatorname{bits}(ab)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Multiplication step]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.mulStep}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.mulStep}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.add, Complexity.isNilB, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Turing.pairEncode}
For a list state $S$, write its nested pair decomposition as $(A,(B,C))$. If $B$ is
empty, the step returns $S$; otherwise it returns the encoding of $(	ext{false} ::
A,(	ext{drop}_1(B),R))$, where $R$ is the binary sum of the encoding of $(C,A)$ when the
first bit of $B$ is true, and is $C$ when that bit is false. An empty $B$ has default
first bit false.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of a Multiplication Step]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_mulStep}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_mulStep}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.mulStep, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_add, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_cons, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_slot2, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_slot3, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_const, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_headD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_id, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_isNil, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_ite, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_tail}
\difficulty{3}
For a bit string $S$, apply the following update: if the first component of the second
component decoded from $S$ is empty, return $S$; otherwise form a new encoded pair whose
first component is $0$ followed by the first decoded component of $S$, and whose second
component encodes the tail and first bit of the first component decoded from the second
component of $S$, together with either the sum of the second decoded component of that
inner pair and the first decoded component of $S$ when that first bit is $1$, or the
remaining second decoded component otherwise. This update function is polynomial-time
computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Multiplication invariant]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.MulInv}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.MulInv}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Turing.pairEncode}
For lists $z$ and $S$, write the defaulted pair decomposition of $z$ as $(X,Y)$. The
multiplication invariant holds when there are lists $A,B,C$ such that $S$ encodes
$(A,(B,C))$, the binary value of $C$ plus the product of the binary values of $A$ and
$B$ equals the product of the binary values of $X$ and $Y$, $C$ is the canonical binary
representation of its value, and the combined lengths of $A$ and $B$ are at most the
combined lengths of $X$ and $Y$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Multiplication invariant under a step]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.mulInv_step}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.mulInv_step}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.MulInv, Complexity.BinArith.add, Complexity.BinArith.bitsVal_eq_headD, Complexity.BinArith.mulStep, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal_bits, Complexity.isNilB, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairFstD_pairEncode, Complexity.pairSndD, Complexity.pairSndD_pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $z$ and $S$ be bit strings, and suppose $S$ satisfies the multiplication invariant
for $z$. Then the state after one multiplication step also satisfies that invariant. If
the first component decoded from the second component of $S$ is nonempty, its length in
the new state is strictly smaller; if it is empty, the step leaves $S$ unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Length bound for multiplication witnesses]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.length_le_of_mulInv}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.length_le_of_mulInv}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.MulInv, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal_lt_two_pow, Complexity.LogProg.length_bits_le, Complexity.length_pair_components_le, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Turing.length_pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $z$ and $S$ be bit strings, and let $u$ and $v$ be the total first and second
projections of $z$. Suppose there are bit strings $A,B,C$ such that $S$ encodes the pair
$(A,	ext{the pair }(B,C))$, the value of $C$ plus the product of the values of $A$ and
$B$ equals the product of the values of $u$ and $v$, $C$ is the canonical bit
representation of its value, and $|A|+|B|\le |u|+|v|$. Then $|S|\le 4(|z|+1)$, where
$|\cdot|$ denotes bit-string length and the value of a bit string is its little-endian
binary value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Multiplication initialization]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.mulInit}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.mulInit}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Turing.pairEncode}
For a list $z$, write its defaulted pair decomposition as $(X,Y)$. The initialization
encodes the nested pair $(X,(Y,[]))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Initial multiplication invariant]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.mulInv_init}

\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.MulInv, Complexity.BinArith.mulInit, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal}
\difficulty{1}

components of $z$ satisfies the multiplication invariant for $z$.

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Computability of Product]
\lean{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_mul}
\label{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_mul}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.MulInv, Complexity.BinArith.iterate_invariant, Complexity.BinArith.iterate_measure_eq_zero, Complexity.BinArith.length_le_of_mulInv, Complexity.BinArith.mul, Complexity.BinArith.mulInit, Complexity.BinArith.mulInv_init, Complexity.BinArith.mulInv_step, Complexity.BinArith.mulStep, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_iterate, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_mulStep, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_slot3, Complexity.LogProg.bitsVal, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.length_pairSndD_le, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairFstD_pairEncode, Complexity.pairSndD, Complexity.pairSndD_pairEncode, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_const, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD}

Encode a pair of bit strings by doubling each bit of the first string, appending the
separator $01$, and then appending the second string. Decode the two components, taking
